docs.title: Project Overview
docs.text:
The Edge Computing Wildlife Monitoring System is a semester-long collaborative project focused on developing a distributed, intelligent wildlife detection solution using edge computing and modern cloud-native technologies. Designed for remote deployment, the system utilizes Raspberry Pi single-board computers equipped with camera module to automatically detect and identify animal species—such as cats, birds, dogs and humans —using object detection models like YOLO and Roboflow.

The sensor node operates independently, performing real-time inference on captured images and transmitting detection data to a central backend system. This backend, deployed on a high-availability Kubernetes cluster of Raspberry Pi 3 devices, handles image storage (via MinIO), data storage (via PostgreSQL), monitoring and system orchestration. A Reactjs-based frontend displays visual insights including, proof images, and log history. Communication between components is facilitated through REST APIs protocols and ClusterIP services.

In addition to monitoring capabilities, the system includes a Telegram bot for real-time notifications upon wildlife detection. This edge-based approach reduces bandwidth usage, supports scalability, and allows for responsive wildlife event tracking. The project aims to explore real-world applications of AI, IoT, and distributed systems while tackling challenges related to performance, reliability, and integration across diverse hardware and software components.

docs.title: Hardware & Architecture
docs.text:
This project is built using a distributed hardware architecture that includes edge computing nodes (Raspberry Pi-based sensor units), a centralized Kubernetes cluster (for backend/frontend deployment and storage), and supporting peripherals. The hardware is designed to be portable, scalable, and suitable for field deployment in outdoor environments.

🧱 1. Hardware Inventory:

The project kit includes the following hardware components:

Quantity Item Description 1x Raspberry Pi 5 (8GB RAM) – Sensor Node 1x Raspberry Pi 4 – Optional secondary sensor node or edge processing 6x Raspberry Pi 3 – Kubernetes Cluster nodes 1x Logitech Camera Module (12MP) 1x Google Coral USB Accelerator (for ML inference acceleration) 1x Gigabit Ethernet Switch 9x RJ45 Ethernet Cables 10x MicroSD Cards (32GB each) 1x USB 3.0 SD/MicroSD Card Reader 3x SD Card Adapters 1x Raspberry Pi 27W USB-C Power Supply 1x Raspberry Pi 15W USB-C Power Supply 1x Anker 60W USB Power Supply Hub 6x Micro USB Power Cables 60x M2.5 Spacer Bolts 1x USB A - USB C Adapter 1x Aluminum Carrying Case (460x340x160 mm)

🖼️ 2. System Layout:

The hardware system is split into two major components:

A. Sensor Node(s):

  1. Raspberry Pi4(Primary)
  2. Camera Module connected
  3. Google Coral USB Accelerator connected via USB 3.0
  4. Runs object detection locally using YOLO/Roboflow
  5. Sends detection events (REST) to backend

B. Kubernetes Cluster:

5x Raspberry Pi 3 Boards and 1x Raspberry pi 4 form a k3s-based HA Kubernetes Cluster.

Deployed components:

  1. Backend API services (ExpressJS)
  2. Frontend (Reactjs)
  3. Object storage (MinIO with S3 API)
  4. Data Storage(PostgreSQL)
  5. Monitoring(Prometheus,Grafana,Helm charts)

Power and network managed via Anker power hub and Ethernet switch.

🔗 3. Connectivity & Networking:

  1. All devices are interconnected via the Gigabit Ethernet switch.
  2. Using laptop as a ISP.
  3. Static IP configuration using netstat.
  4. Sensor nodes and cluster nodes communicate over LAN using REST.

docs.title: Software Stack
docs.text:
The software stack is designed to provide a robust, scalable, and efficient wildlife monitoring solution, leveraging modern frameworks, machine learning libraries, and containerized deployment on Raspberry Pi devices.

  1. Operating Systems:

  2. Sensor Node (Raspberry Pi 5)

Raspberry Pi OS Desktop (64-bit): Debian-based OS optimized for Raspberry Pi hardware, providing stable support for camera modules and peripheral drivers.

  • Kubernetes Cluster Nodes (Master- Raspberry pi 4 & Workers - Raspberry Pi 3):

Ubuntu 22.04 LTS (64-bit): Long Term Support version offering robustness, security updates, and wide community support for Kubernetes and containerized environments.

  1. Edge Computing & Object Detection (Sensor Node):

  2. RoboFlow: For training and running lightweight object detection models optimized for edge inference on Raspberry Pi OS.

  3. YOLO (You Only Look Once): Real-time object detection framework (YOLOv8), adapted for Raspberry Pi OS and optimized for Coral USB Accelerator.

  4. Google Coral USB Accelerator: Provides Edge TPU acceleration for TensorFlow Lite models to boost inference speed on the sensor node.

  5. OpenCV: For handling camera input, image pre-processing, and post-processing on the sensor node.

  6. Backend & Cluster (Ubuntu 22.04 LTS Nodes):

  7. K3s (Lightweight Kubernetes Distribution): Runs on Ubuntu 22.04 to orchestrate backend, frontend, storage, and messaging services across the Raspberry Pi 3 cluster.

  8. Containers: Container runtime for deploying microservices in the Kubernetes cluster.

  9. JavaScript(ExpressJS): REST API development framework for backend services that manage sensor data ingestion, node management, and event logging.

  10. Database (PostgreSQL): To store the timestamps and unique id, path for detected images.

  11. Object Storage: Minio deployed as distributed storage compatible with S3 API for storing images, logs, and metadata.

  12. Frontend (Ubuntu 22.04 LTS Nodes):

  13. React.js: Frontend framework for creating the web dashboard presenting event logs, images, timestamps, and an interactive map.

  14. Docker containers: The frontend is containerized and deployed on the Kubernetes cluster.

  15. Notifications:

  16. Telegram Bot API: Used to send real-time notifications about detected wildlife events to users.

  17. Development & DevOps Tools:

  18. Git & GitHub: Source control and collaboration.

  19. K3S: Command-line Kubernetes tool for cluster management on Ubuntu nodes.

  20. Visual Studio Code: Recommended IDE with plugins for Python, Docker, Kubernetes.

docs.title: Sensor Node
docs.text: This section covers the complete configuration of the sensor node using Raspberry Pi 4, camera module, and PyCoral for edge inference.

docs.title: 1. Raspberry Pi OS Installation
docs.text:
• Device: Raspberry Pi 4
  • Operating System: Raspberry Pi OS (64-bit) – Desktop(bookworm)

Steps:

  • Use the Raspberry Pi Imager to flash Raspberry Pi OS (Desktop 64-bit) onto a 32GB microSD card.
  • After flashing, boot the Pi and complete the initial setup:
  • Set up Wi-Fi or Ethernet
  • Configure locale and keyboard layout
  • Enable SSH (optional)
  • Update system packages

docs.title: 2. Camera Module Setup
docs.text:
• Connect the Camera Modul to the CSI port on the Raspberry Pi.

  • Enable the camera module using: sudo raspi-config → Interface Options → Camera → Enable

  • Reboot the Raspberry Pi to apply changes.

  • Verify camera functionality using OpenCV or CLI utilities.

docs.title: 3. Model Deployment on Edge (Roboflow SDK)
docs.text:
• Use the Roboflow Python SDK to deploy object detection models on the sensor node.
  • Export trained models in YOLOv8, or Edge TPU-compatible formats.
  • Use the PyCoral SDK to load the model and perform inference on captured images.
  • Models are capable of detecting species such as cats, dogs, birds, and humans etc.

docs.title: 4. Edge Detection Process and Inference Loop
docs.text:
• Images are captured either periodically(e.g., motion detection).
  • Each image is processed by the model.
  • If a valid detection is found:
  • Send detection metadata (category, timestamp, and image-buffer) via REST API to the backend server.

docs.title: 5. Performance Optimization (Coral USB Accelerator)
docs.text:
• For improved performance, a Google Coral USB Accelerator can be used with the Raspberry Pi.
  • Useful when using TensorFlow Lite models compiled for Edge TPU.
  • Installation involves:
  • Adding Coral's APT repository
  • Installing PyCoral runtime and Python bindings
  • Provides significantly faster inference and reduced CPU usage.

Note: Ensure that USB 3.0 ports on the Raspberry Pi 4 are used for connecting the Coral device for maximum performance.

docs.title: 6. Setup
docs.text:
A. System Update

`sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y`

B. Install Python & Virtual Environment

`sudo apt install python3-pip python3-venv -y`

C. Install OpenCV

`sudo apt install libatlas-base-dev libjpeg-dev libqtgui4 libqt4-test -y`
`pip3 install opencv-python`

D. Install Roboflow Python SDK

`pip3 install roboflow`

E. Download and Use Roboflow Model

`Sign in at https://app.roboflow.com`

After training your model, go to the Deploy tab

Select YOLOv5 export

Use the following Python snippet to load and run inference on your edge device:

from roboflow import Roboflow rf = Roboflow(api_key="your_api_key") project = rf.workspace("your_workspace").project("your_project") model = project.version("x").model prediction = model.predict("your_image.jpg").json()

F. Coral USB Accelerator (Optional)

If your Roboflow model is exported to TensorFlow Lite and Edge TPU format:

echo "deb https://packages.cloud.google.com/apt coral-edgetpu-stable main" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/coral-edgetpu.list curl https://packages.cloud.google.com/apt/doc/apt-key.gpg | sudo apt-key add - sudo apt update sudo apt install libedgetpu1-std python3-edgetpu -y

G. Camera Enablement

`sudo raspi-config → Interface Options → Enable Camera`
`Reboot the Pi`

H. Telegram Notifications

docs.title: Object Detection & Model
docs.text: This section describes the full workflow for obtaining images, annotating them, training an object detection model using Roboflow, and preparing it for deployment on the Raspberry Pi sensor node.

docs.title: 1. Species Selection
docs.text:
Identify at least three target animal species for monitoring. Examples include:

  • 🐈 Cats
  • 🐕 Dogs
  • 🐦 Birds
  • 🦔 Hedgehogs
  • 🐁 Mice
  • 🐀 Rats

Ensure the selected classes are distinct in visual features and relevant to your target habitat.

docs.title: 2. Data Collection (Kaggle & Pexels)
docs.text: Instead of collecting data with hardware, use high-quality public image datasets.

docs.title: 📦 Sources:
docs.text:
• 🧠 Kaggle Datasets
  • Visit https://www.kaggle.com/datasets and search for species-specific datasets (e.g., “cat and dog dataset”, “bird detection”)

  • Download relevant image datasets as .zip files

  • 📸 Pexels API / Website

  • Visit https://www.pexels.com/search/cat/ (replace “cat” with your species)
  • You can use the Pexels API to download copyright-free, labeled images:
    • https://www.pexels.com/api/

Organize the collected data into directories by class:

📁 dataset/ ├── cat/ ├── dog/ └── bird/

Note: Ensure all images are clear, high-resolution, and representative of real-world conditions.

docs.title: 3. Image Annotation
docs.text:
1. Image Annotation & Labeling: Label images for object detection, classification, and segmentation with a user-friendly interface.

  2. Dataset Preprocessing & Augmentation: improve model performance with built-in tools like rotation, flipping, noise, blur, and more.

  3. Model Training (AutoML): Train computer vision models without code using Roboflow Train, or export datasets to use with YOLO, TensorFlow, etc.

  4. Model evaluation & Metrics: Get performance insights through precision, recall, mAP, and visualize model results easily.

  5. Deployment via API & Edge Devices: Deploy trained models to edge devices like Raspberry Pi or Jetson.

  6. Dataset Versioning & Management: Track changes with version control, manage large datasets efficiently, and collaborate with teams.

  7. Data Insights & Labeling Analytics.

docs.title: 4. Dataset Organization
docs.text:
Use Roboflow to split the dataset:

  • 70% Training Set
  • 20% Validation Set
  • 10% Test Set

Roboflow handles augmentation and labeling format conversions automatically.

docs.title: 5. Model Training (Using Roboflow)
docs.text:
Choose a suitable model architecture (e.g., YOLOv8) in Roboflow.

Training includes:

  • Data preprocessing and augmentation
  • Iterative learning with validation feedback
  • Metric monitoring (mAP, Precision, Recall)

No local GPU required — training is cloud-hosted.

Step 1: Export Dataset from Roboflow

• Go to your Roboflow project.

• Click "Export".

• Choose the YOLOv8 format.

• Click "Download ZIP".

Step 2: Upload ZIP to Google Drive

• Open Google Drive.

• Create a new folder, e.g., roboflow_yolov8_dataset.

• Upload the ZIP file into that folder.

from google.colab import drive drive.mount('/content/drive') # Use drive directly since you imported it previously

Step 3: Open Google Colab

• Go to Google Colab.

• Create a new notebook.

• Mount your Google Drive

Step 4: Unzip Dataset

• In the Colab notebook, unzip your Roboflow dataset into a folder inside Google Drive.

• This will create folders like train/images, train/labels, valid/images, etc.

Step 5: Check the data.yaml File

• Make sure the data.yaml file inside the unzipped folder points to the correct folders in Google Drive.

• You may need to adjust the paths to match where your images and labels are located.

Step 6: Install YOLOv8 (Ultralytics)

• In the Colab notebook, install the Ultralytics package to use YOLOv8.

docs.title: Install the ultralytics package within the same cell where it is imported
docs.text: !pip install ultralytics --upgrade

docs.title: Now import ultralytics
docs.text:
import ultralytics

Step 7: Train the YOLOv8 Model

• Use the YOLOv8 training command (you just provide the path to the data.yaml file and a model like yolov8n.pt).

• The training will use the images and labels stored in Google Drive.

model.train( epochs=300, batch=64, imgsz=640, device=0, lr0=0.01, patience=50, project=os.path.join(dataset_path, 'runs'), name='yolov8_model_nms', exist_ok=True )

Step8: Model Validation(using roboflow)

After training the YOLOv8 model, validation was performed using the best model checkpoint: /content/drive/MyDrive/animals/runs/yolov8_model_nms/weights/best.pt

The validation was conducted using Ultralytics YOLOv8 v8.3.152 with the following system setup:

• Python Version: 3.11.13

• Torch Version: 2.6.0+cu124

• GPU: NVIDIA A100-SXM4-40GB (CUDA)

🔍 Model Summary

• Total Layers: 72

• Parameters: 3,006,428

• GFLOPs: 8.1

• Gradients: 0 (fused model)

⚡ Performance Speed

• Preprocessing: 0.1 ms/image

• Inference: 0.5 ms/image

• Loss Calculation: 0.0 ms/image

• Postprocessing: 2.2 ms/image

✅ Interpretation

The model achieved strong performance across all classes, particularly on Cat and Dog categories, with mAP@0.5 values above 0.99. The overall mAP@0.5 is 0.949, indicating high object detection accuracy. Slightly lower recall and mAP@0.5:0.95 in Bird and Person classes suggest opportunities for improvement through additional training data or targeted augmentation.

docs.title: 📊 Validation Metrics
docs.text:
Class Images Instances Precision (P) Recall (R) mAP@0.5 mAP@0.5:0.95 All 301 844 0.958 0.885 0.94 0.809 Cat 59 64 0.992 1.000 0.995 0.972 Dog 86 108 0.984 0.981 0.987 0.956 Bird 78 231 0.939 0.793 0.879 0.657 Person 78 441 0.916 0.765 0.9 0.652

Step:9 model export:

After completing the training phase, the trained model was exported using Roboflow’s export tools for deployment and inference. The model was exported in the YOLOv8 PyTorch format, optimized for CPU-based inference. Additionally, an optional export format was available via Roboflow Lite, which supports Edge TPU devices such as the Google Coral USB Accelerator.

📦 Export Formats

• YOLOv8 PyTorch (.pt): Suitable for deployment on systems using Python and PyTorch.

• TensorFlow Lite (.tflite): Lightweight version for inference on edge devices (optional).

🧾 Exported Assets Provided by Roboflow

• Model Weights: .pt or .tflite file depending on the selected format.

• Inference Script: A ready-to-use Python script for running the model on new images or video streams.

• Class Names & Label Map: Files mapping class indices to human-readable labels, essential for interpreting predictions.

This export process simplifies integration into applications, allowing for flexible deployment across a range of platforms—from local machines to embedded edge devices.

# Define the path to a dataset YAML or a calibration dataset

data_yaml = "/content/drive/MyDrive/animals/config.yaml" 

    # dataset config with paths to images (for calibration)

    # Export the model to TFLite with INT8 quantization

model.export(

`format="tflite",  # target format`

`int8=True,        # enable INT8 post-training quantization`

`data=data_yaml,   # provide dataset for calibration`

`imgsz=640         # image size`

)

docs.text: Bot setup steps:

docs.title: Low Level Diagram

Telegram Bot API integration:

Step-1: Use the @BotFather bot in Telegram application to register bot and receive its authentication token.

Step-2: Get the Telegram Chat IDs from the people whom you want to share the notification with.

Step-3: User the /sendPhoto api of Telegram to send the Photo or use /sendMessage api to send just an text message.

Event trigger conditions:

Condition-1: If the sensor-node captures the wildlife detection then the server triggers the telegramService to send the image and the caption.

Condition-2: If the github action pipeline detects the changes in frontend or server or k3s directory of the repository then it triggers the notification.

2. Software Issues: * OS crashes or instability * Camera module driver problems * Compatibility with YOLO * Issue in installing PYcoral(because of dependency of gdal)

3. ML Model Issues:

  • GPU-Related Error in YOLOv8:

RuntimeError: CUDA out of memory

This error occurred when the model tried to allocate more GPU memory than was available. It is commonly triggered by:

• Large batch sizes or input image dimensions,

• High model complexity,

• Insufficient GPU memory (e.g., <8GB VRAM).

• RuntimeError: CUDA out of memory

→ Model, batch size, or image size too large for available GPU memory.

• ZeroDivisionError: division by zero

→ Usually due to empty validation set or no detections.

• FileNotFoundError

→ Image or label paths missing or misconfigured in data.yaml.

• Unsupported Export Formats:

Some target platforms did not support the exported model formats directly, leading to conversion failures or compatibility issues.

• Quantization Limitations:

Converting the model to lower-precision formats (e.g., for TensorRT or Edge TPU) introduced quantization challenges, which affected model accuracy or caused export failures.

• Hardware Compatibility Issues: Inference on certain edge devices failed due to precision mismatches (e.g., float32 vs. int8), requiring additional post-processing or model optimization steps.

• Incompatible Output Tensor Format for Coral Edge TPU During deployment of the YOLOv8 model to the Coral Edge TPU, a compatibility issue was encountered. The exported TensorFlow Lite (TFLite) model produced a single raw output tensor, which does not meet the Coral TPU’s requirement for object detection. Specifically, the Coral Edge TPU expects models to output four distinct tensors:

• boxes – bounding box coordinates

• classes – detected class indices

• scores – confidence scores

• num_detections – total number of valid detections

Proposed Solutions:

  1. Re-export the model with NMS = True This integrates the post-processing step into the model itself, producing the required four-output tensor structure compatible with Coral TPU.

  2. Apply manual NMS in Python after inference if re-exporting isn’t possible.If re-exporting is not feasible, apply manual Non-Max Suppression (NMS) in the host system after inference. This involves parsing the raw output tensor and filtering overlapping bounding boxes using Intersection-over-Union (IoU) metrics in Python.

4. Networking and Cluster Setup:

  • How to use Laptop as a Router?

In order connect all the Raspberry Pi Machines using Network Switch we need to have a router to act as a Network Provider. Incase of no router availability, it is possible to use the Laptop as a router.

Here we're using Windows-11 based Laptop as a Router.

Step-1: Press Windows + R

Step-2: Run ncpa.cpl

Step-3: Make sure there are two adapter(s), Ethernet and Wifi.

Step-4: Optional Reset all the network configuration and restart system.

Step-5: Right click on the Wifi Adapter and open the Properties.

Step-6: In the sharing tab, just enable the option: Allow other network users to connect through this computer's network connection

Step-7: Press Ok and save the settings.

Now, Wifi-adapter will automatically assign the IP address like 192.168.137.1 with subnet mask 255.255.255.0

  • Node joining issues: DNS Issue(s) in Nodes k3s cluster's master-node was not able to pull any images from the docker-hub due to DNS issues because on all nodes DNS was linked to system-d-resolved which was not allowing the nodes to access the hosts outside the cluster.

Steps for the Solution:

Run command: sudo ln -sf /run/systemd/resolve/resolv.conf /etc/resolv.conf

Then run: sudo cat /etc/resolv.conf

Add in the file: $ nameserver 8.8.8.8

$ nameserver 1.1.1.1

$ search .

Save the file and restart the deployment.

minioClient.setBucketPolicy(env.MINIO_BUCKET, JSON.stringify(policy), function (err) { if (err) return console.log("Error setting policy:", err); console.log("Public read policy applied."); });
